paras: The killing of Will Smith was the fatal shooting of a Black chicken seller in Memphis, Tennessee, by grocer Lewis G. Slaughter on the morning of August 29, 1903, while Slaughter guarded him at the order of an off-duty patrolman. Patrolman A. S. Boyles had handed Slaughter his pistol with instructions to kill the prisoner if he tried to escape, and Smith died at the city hospital several days later. The case drew notice because the white Memphis Commercial Appeal investigated it, exposed Boyles's false first report, and denounced the killing as cold-blooded, coverage that was reprinted in both the white and the Black press.

Smith had been going from house to house on Walker avenue selling chickens, and the Commercial Appeal described him as harmless, perhaps a man from the country. Boyles, who was off duty and at work building a house, accused him of being a thief selling stolen chickens, fetched his pistol, and arrested him. Neighbors later said Boyles roomed across the street from Slaughter's store and was Slaughter's friend.

Boyles took Smith to Slaughter's grocery and barroom at 1077 Walker avenue, at the corner of Elmwood, and left to put on his uniform. By his own account he told Slaughter, 'If this man tries to get away from you, kill him.' Slaughter shot Smith in front of the store, and a small boy on the porch was knocked down as the wounded man fell on him. Witnesses reported that Boyles asked over the body, 'Well, you got him, didn't you?' and that Slaughter answered with a smile; one neighbor said that when she asked Slaughter why he had done it, he only laughed.

Smith was taken to the city hospital, where, according to a Memphis dispatch dated September 3, he died about 11 o'clock the previous morning. A statement taken from him before he died was said to agree with the eyewitnesses.

Boyles first reported to his superiors that he had shot Smith himself, and admitted that Slaughter fired only after the Commercial Appeal published its account. Acting police chief O. H. Perry said the department would await the coroner's inquest before arresting anyone, while officers looked into the dead man's record and found nothing. Deputy Coroner Ernst Miller impaneled a jury, but testimony was postponed because the principal witnesses were absent, and no verdict appears in the coverage.

Neighbors who had not known Smith were reported incensed, and the Commercial Appeal listed several, including a deaf man who lived next door, as ready to testify that Slaughter fired. By early October, Black ministers in Memphis were appealing for $500 to hire a white lawyer for the case, though the city's correspondent to the Colored American expected little response. No report of an arrest, indictment, or trial was found.

Most coverage came from the Commercial Appeal, whose editorial 'In Darkest Memphis' the Indianapolis Journal reprinted on September 10 under the subhead 'The Manner in Which a Tennessee Policeman Enforces the Law.' The editorial opened by saying the life of a 'negro' in Memphis was 'so valueless that it is freely taken without fear of future punishment,' mocked Boyles as incompetent, and demanded that the coroner act, while still calling the victim 'low-browed' and 'unthinking.'

Two days later the Baltimore Afro-American filled part of its front page with the Commercial Appeal's news investigation under a headline describing an 'Invollensive [Inoffensive] Negro Shot Down In Cold Blood.' That copy stressed that the grand jury would not ask whether Smith had been a chicken thief, answering the police inquiry into his record. The Colored American's Memphis correspondent went further, writing that Boyles acted on the idea that a Black man had no right to own chickens and calling the killing 'one of the many brutal murders' committed in the South.

Boyles said Smith jumped up and broke for the door before Slaughter fired. Neighbors named by the Commercial Appeal said Smith made no attempt to escape and was shot without provocation. Boyles also gave differing reasons for first claiming the shot: that he felt as responsible as if he had fired, or, according to Perry, that he wished to protect Slaughter and thought Smith was not badly hurt.

reader.title: Killing of Will Smith
bases: An off-duty patrolman arrested Smith, handed his pistol to a grocer with orders to kill the prisoner if he tried to escape, and the grocer shot him while he was in that custody (A1, A2, A7).

The Commercial Appeal's news and editorial reports (reprinted in A1 and A2-A5), the patrolman's own interview (A1), and a separate Memphis Black correspondent (A7) agree that Slaughter shot Smith while guarding him for Boyles; they differ only on whether Smith tried to escape.

accounts.label: Patrolman Boyles's account
accounts.gist: Boyles said Smith jumped up and broke for the door, and Slaughter took his order to shoot literally and fired; he said he first claimed the shot because he considered himself responsible.

accounts.label: Acting chief Perry's account of Boyles
accounts.gist: Perry said Boyles claimed the shot to protect Slaughter, believing Smith was not seriously wounded.

accounts.label: Eyewitnesses (via the Commercial Appeal)
accounts.gist: Neighbors said Smith did not run and was shot without provocation, that a child was in the line of fire, and that Boyles and Slaughter spoke callously over the body.

accounts.label: Dying statement
accounts.gist: A statement taken from Smith before his death was said to corroborate the eyewitnesses; its text is not reprinted.

accounts.label: Black Memphis correspondent
accounts.gist: Residents named in the Commercial Appeal said Smith made no attempt to escape and was shot on the platform without provocation.

framing.detail: The Indianapolis Journal reprinted the Commercial Appeal editorial 'In Darkest Memphis,' which said Smith was 'shot down in cold blood' and called Boyles incompetent, while also calling the victim 'low-browed' and 'unthinking.'
The Afro-American ran the Commercial Appeal's investigation on its front page under a headline calling Smith 'An Invollensive [Inoffensive] Negro Shot Down In Cold Blood.'
The Colored American's Memphis correspondent called it 'one of the many brutal murders' in the South and doubted white Memphis would punish a white man.
